Immunohistochemistry was positive for SOX10, Melan-A and S100 — a melanocytic profile diagnostic of melanoma — and negative for calretinin, WT1 and EMA, which excludes malignant mesothelioma, and negative for p40, excluding squamous carcinoma. The pleural involvement with nodular circumferential thickening and effusion explains the reduced left basal breath sounds, while diffuse fine crackles and disproportionate hypoxemia reflect associated pulmonary lymphangitic carcinomatosis. The rapid one-week symptomatic course with normal inflammatory markers is typical of aggressive lymphangitic/pleural malignant spread rather than infection.

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: This is stage IV disease. Management requires urgent oncology referral, completion of staging (PET-CT and brain MRI, as melanoma has high CNS tropism), and molecular profiling for BRAF V600, NRAS and KIT mutations to determine eligibility for targeted therapy, alongside consideration of immune checkpoint inhibition. Repeat thoracentesis or an indwelling pleural catheter/pleurodesis may be needed for symptomatic relief of the recurrent effusion.
